# **Introduction and Introduction (Preface)**

**The importance of this lecture: The interview/pitch is the final key link that can best demonstrate your "execution and implementation ability"**  
Even if you have prepared a detailed business plan, the interview and roadshow are still crucial. The guarantee agency will evaluate your **ability** as a founder, your **deep understanding** of the project itself, and your **true intention** to start a business in the United Kingdom through this face-to-face communication. This means that the interview is not only to review your written materials, but also to examine whether you can **prove that you are the leader and actual executor of the plan** . You need to **express yourself truthfully** , demonstrate control of project details, clear interpretation of data, and in-depth understanding of the United Kingdom market.

# **Menu design**

## **Why Learn**

In this lecture, you will delve into how to effectively prepare and present your business ideas, especially during key interviews and roadshows with guarantee agencies and potential investors. Mastering these skills is crucial for the successful application of the United Kingdom Innovative Founder Visa and every step of your future entrepreneurship.

* **Understand the true evaluation logic of the guarantee agency interview** The guarantee agency interview is a key link to evaluate your "execution and landing ability". Its success rate depends not only on the quality of your written materials, but also on the **authenticity and credibility** of your story. The interview aims to verify whether you really **understand the project** , are the **leader and actual executor of the plan** , and evaluate your **ability** and the **true intention** of starting a business in the United Kingdom. You will understand how the reviewer judges whether you have **founder thinking** through questions (such as pricing, user sources, data basis), rather than just "being packaged to apply for a visa".  
* **Familiarize yourself with typical questions that may be asked and the intention behind them** We will sort out the most commonly asked questions by guarantee agencies, covering more than 20 key points such as project overview, innovation, business model, team capabilities, market analysis, and development plans in the UK. You will not only know what the question is, but also understand the true intention behind the question (for example, asking about the derivation method of the market ceiling is to evaluate your computational rigor; asking about team capabilities is to evaluate whether you match the project requirements).  
* **Learn to organize your answer structure and expression logic efficiently** You will learn **The three core principles of "telling a good story"** :  
  * **Sense of substitution** : Use **user perspective** to tell stories, concretize abstract concepts, and let the audience quickly understand the product value and user experience.  
  * **Logic** : Choose **a complete storyline** (such as chronological or top-down logic), push it layer by layer, confirm it repeatedly, and ensure that investors gradually understand and agree with your value.  
  * **Highlights** : Using techniques such as reversal, analogy, and the "In-Out sentence structure", make your story more engaging and improve from "qualified" to "excellent". You will also learn how to avoid getting too caught up in details and instead **give conclusions first, then develop arguments** , improving communication efficiency.  
* **Master interview adaptation and on-site coping strategies** We will teach the "six no principles" of roadshow communication to help you cope with the interview calmly:  
  * **Not rigid** : Flexibly adjust the narrative rhythm and depth, and explain **user-centered** based on investors' interests and understanding of the industry.  
  * **Not sad or overbearing** : maintain an equal dialogue mentality, avoid overconfidence or blindly cater, and sincerely communicate business.  
  * **Do not debate** : view communication as a seminar rather than a debate, seek common ground while reserving differences for minor differences, and stop at the right time for major differences to find the next opportunity.  
  * **Not always interrupted** : Take control of the narrative thread, effectively handle interruptions, and ensure that key information is fully conveyed.  
  * **Do not belittle competitors** : objectively analyze the competitive environment, highlight their own differentiated play and advantages, rather than blindly belittle opponents.  
  * **Don't get caught up in details too early** : tell the story from macro to micro, and avoid getting caught up in trivial disputes at the beginning.  
* **Polish your business pitch structure with a telling approach** You'll learn how to build a compelling business roadshow:  
  * Understanding the core elements of the Pitch Deck requires answering four core questions: "What market opportunity do you see?", "What is the company building?", "How will the company grow?" **and** "Why are you and your team the best candidates?"  
  * Master the writing methods of "two-page" (two-pager) **and** "one-sentence introduction" (Elevator Pitch) **,** "project recommendation letter" (PitchWords). These concise materials can help you efficiently attract investors' interest in a limited time and convey the innovation, feasibility and scalability of the project.  
  * Learn how to effectively present products, such as through **demo photos, videos, or graphic samples** , rather than lengthy video demonstrations, to better help interviewers understand the value and user experience of the product.

## **Warm-up thinking question**

Before entering the formal course content, let's first use a few warm-up questions to test your preliminary understanding and preparation for the interview and roadshow.  
![][image4]

### **Thinking Question 1: In the interview, the evaluator values your "content" or "expression" more ?**

In an interview with a guarantor agency, **both content (your business plan, data, and project potential) and presentation (your communication style and credibility) are crucial, but presentation is the bridge that allows content to be effectively evaluated** .

* **Expression is the key to verifying the content** : Even if your business plan is well written and the project has potential, if in the interview **unclear expression, inadequate preparation, or leaving an unprofessional impression** , you may still be rejected. The interview is not only to review written materials, but also to examine whether you can **prove that you are the leader and actual executor of the plan** . The reviewer of the visa guarantee agency will judge whether you have \*\* "founder's thinking" **through questioning, rather than just** "being packaged to apply for a visa" \*\*.  
* **Clear expression reflects true understanding** : Vague expression can make it difficult for endorsing agencies to determine whether you truly understand the project or are "riding on hot words" (such as AI, NFT, etc.). Innovation visa requires you to be able to solve real problems more effectively with new methods and have commercial feasibility, which means you must be "better than the existing \+ able to express this clearly".  
* **Natural expression demonstrates internalized thinking** : If you read a business plan or roadshow presentation throughout, the content will appear formatted, stiff, and emotionless, which will be considered to lack internalized thinking and a real sense of leadership. The interview evaluates whether you really understand these logics, not what you can memorize. Therefore, **authentic and credible expression** is the core influencing factor of success rate.

![][image5]

### **Question 2: If you are asked, "Please briefly introduce your project," can you explain it clearly, accurately, and attractively in 2 minutes ?**

**Yes, this is not only possible, but also a crucial ability** . Although the guarantee agency's meeting agenda will set aside 10 minutes of roadshow time for your project overview, you also need to prepare a more refined version, such as **a 1-minute elevator pitch** .

* **Refine the core message** : Your opening introduction should immediately capture the reviewer's point of interest and clearly explain your business in concise language (such as a 5-7 word brief).  
* **Highlight your value proposition** : A one-minute video presentation should clearly communicate your business idea, the problem you solve, and what makes your solution unique.  
* **Efficiently attract interest** : Whether it is \*\* "a one-sentence introduction" **or** "PitchWords" (PitchWords) **, the goal is to attract the reviewers' interest in the shortest possible time and convey the innovation, feasibility and scalability of the project. This means that you need to** tell a story from the user's perspective, be logical, and use skills to highlight the highlights \*\*.  
* **State the conclusion first and then expand** : In a short period of time, it is recommended that you "state the conclusion first, and then provide evidence to support the conclusion" to avoid getting stuck in details too early, thus improving communication efficiency.

![][image6]

### **Question 3: Why do judges always "ask for details" and "why"? Are you ready ?**

The reason why the reviewers of the visa guarantee agency always like to "ask for details" and "why" is to **deeply verify your true ability as a founder, the depth of understanding and actual control of the project** .

* **Verify founder thinking and leadership** : The reviewer will judge whether you have founder thinking and whether you have truly led the development of the business model by asking about details such as project pricing, user sources, and data basis. For example, asking about the calculation method of the market ceiling is to evaluate the rigor of your calculation.  
* **Assessing Risk Response and Iteration Capabilities** : When your answers to potential issues (such as poor customer feedback or lower-than-expected conversion rates) are superficial, the reviewer will conclude that you lack specific response measures and product iteration capabilities. Asking for details can reflect your anticipation of risks and preparation for solutions.  
* **Clarify "gray areas" and demonstrate clear thinking** : The parts of the business plan that have not been fully developed, such as early user acquisition, partnerships, etc. \*\* "gray areas" \*\*, the interview is a good supplementary opportunity. The reviewer asks for these details to judge whether your thinking is clear and whether preliminary preparation work has been carried out.  
* **Confirm independent judgment and decision-making ability** : The reviewer will ask you what information you mainly referred to when deciding on the project, and which key decisions you made personally. If you rely too much on external resources (such as business consultants or market reports) and lack clear self-judgment, you may be seen as an executor rather than a leader. Key decisions such as business models, pricing methods, and cooperation strategies should be led by the applicant.

**You need to prepare for these details** :

# **Main Course 1: Interview**

The interview of the Innovation Visa Guarantee Agency is far more than just verifying the content of the business plan. Its core purpose is to **deeply verify the authenticity of the applicant as a founder and the actual execution ability of the business plan** . The reviewer aims to judge whether you have the qualities to lead and promote the project landing through a series of questions and observations.

## **The Essential Logic of Guarantee Interview**

The Core Logic Behind the Endorsement Interview  
The essential logic of a guarantee interview can be summarized into the following three core verification objectives:

### **1\. You are the real founder (Genuine Founder) :**

* The interviewer needs to confirm that you are the **leader and actual executor** of the business plan, not just an applicant "packaged to apply for a visa".  
* They will assess whether you have a **founder mindset** and demonstrate **independent judgment and decision-making ability** .  
* During the interview, the reviewer will judge whether you truly understand the business logic through your **natural expression** , rather than "reading the business plan or roadshow presentation throughout the process", because this may be seen as a lack of internalized thinking and real leadership.  
* Your entrepreneurial motivation should also be clear to avoid being interpreted as a signal **of "starting a business for immigration"** .

### **2\. You can deeply grasp the business details (Business Ownership) :**

* Reviewers will **ask for details** , such as the project's **pricing method, user source, calculation logic and source basis for key data** . This aims to verify your understanding of the business depth.  
* You must be able to **clearly and specifically articulate the "innovation" of the project** , explaining how your plan is **"better than the existing one"** , and "why others can't do it" or "why users will switch to your set".  
* The interview is also a good opportunity for you **to supplement the "gray areas" in the business plan** (such as early user acquisition methods, partnership progress), showing that you have clear thinking and have made preliminary preparations.  
* Key decisions, such as **business models, pricing methods, cooperation strategies,** etc., should be led by the applicant, and excessive reliance on external resources will be seen as a lack of self-judgment.

### **3\. Your execution landing logic is credible and feasible (Execution Confidence) :**

* Reviewers assess your **risk response and product iteration capabilities** for potential issues. When asked about poor customer feedback or lower-than-expected conversion rates, provide specific responses rather than vague answers.  
* This includes showing how you **achieved your first year goals** as well as **your business plan and milestones for the next three years** .  
* You need to clearly explain how **revenue forecasts** are calculated and explain your **market size estimates (TAM/SAM/SOM)** .  
* You also need to elaborate on customer acquisition channels, profit models, team recruitment plans, and specific strategies for developing in the United Kingdom to demonstrate that your business plan is credible and feasible at a practical level.

## **Process of Guaranteed Interview**

The Endorsement Interview Process  
Before arranging an interview, your business plan will undergo multiple rounds of evaluation. First, the guarantee agency will conduct a preliminary review of your business plan and financial plan. If the preliminary review is successful, it will be reviewed by a second evaluator. Only when both evaluators approve of your business plan will an interview be arranged with you to discuss the content of the business plan in more detail. The purpose of the interview is to verify the authenticity and feasibility of the business plan.

### **Preparation before the interview**

You need to prepare the following:

* **Prepare a 10-minute refined presentation (Pitch)** : This presentation needs to highlight the **innovation (innovative)** , **feasibility (viable)** and **scalability (scalable)** . Be sure to strictly control the time, as the meeting agenda is tight.  
* **In-depth understanding of your business plan** : The interview is not just about memorizing the content of the business plan. The reviewer will ask questions about your **pricing strategy** , **user acquisition channels** , **data sources and calculation logic** (such as revenue forecasts). You must be able to clearly and specifically explain **innovation points** , explain how your plan is "better than the existing one" **, and** "why others can't do it" **or** "why users will switch to your system". Unclear explanations of key data or excessive reliance on external consultants' answers will be seen as a lack of leadership in the business model.  
* **Think about risk response strategies** : If customer feedback is poor or conversion rates are lower than expected, you need specific responses rather than vague answers, which reflects your **risk response and product iteration capabilities** .  
* **Clarify entrepreneurial motivation** : Your reasons for choosing to start a business in the United Kingdom should focus on business opportunities and the fit of the project with the United Kingdom market, avoiding giving signals of "starting a business for immigration".

### **Example of Interview Process**

According to the provided meeting agenda, this Zoom video conference usually lasts about 30 minutes. It aims to allow the evaluator to introduce themselves, explain the guarantee process, clarify expectations and requirements, and provide you with the opportunity to present business ideas and answer questions.  
The following is the specific agenda of the meeting and the key points you should pay attention to:

1. **Introductions \- 5 minutes**  
   1. This is your opportunity to establish initial contact with the evaluator. Briefly introduce yourself and your company, and prepare for the following detailed introduction. Maintain a confident and professional attitude.  
   2. Although this part is about introducing each other, be prepared to quickly grab each other's attention with a sentence or paragraph, and extract the brightest point of the project.  
2. **Brief on Process & Support Services from endorsing bodies \- 10 minutes**  
   1. This section mainly introduces the process of guarantee agencies and the support services they can provide.  
   2. You should listen carefully to understand the next steps and available resources. This will also help you understand the reviewers' concerns and their expectations for innovative projects.  
3. **Your Overview \- 10 minutes**  
   1. This is the key moment for you to present your core business idea, the **10-minute refined presentation** you prepare.  
   2. You need to clearly articulate the **problem** you want to solve, your **solution** and its **innovation** , **market opportunities** and **business model** .  
   3. Emphasize how your project is **innovative, feasible, and scalable** . Avoid reading a business plan or roadshow presentation all the way, instead show **internalized thinking and real ownership** of the business.  
   4. If your product has prototypes, MVPs, or early adopters, be sure to provide proof of how it works.  
4. **Q & A Session (Questions) \- 5 minutes**  
   1. Although the time is short, this part is an opportunity for the evaluator to directly verify your understanding of the project.  
   2. They may ask questions about the "gray areas" in your business plan, such as how to acquire early users and initial contact with partner companies.  
   3. You need to demonstrate **independent judgment and decision-making ability** , clearly indicating which decisions in the business plan are made by you personally, and the basis for making these judgments.  
   4. When answering questions, follow the principle of "no debate" **, communicate with an open mind, seek consensus even if there are differences, instead of trying to persuade all investors. At the same time,** respect competitors, objectively analyze the competitive environment, instead of belittling them to elevate oneself.

### **Core Considerations in Interviews**

Throughout the entire interview process, the psychological logic behind the reviewer can be summarized as "trust" in the following three core dimensions:

* **Trust your professionalism** : Are you familiar with every business plan detail, including pricing, user sources, key data calculation logic, and a deep understanding of the industry status quo, development trends, and competition landscape?  
* **Trust your execution** : Whether your business plan is realistic and actionable, including specific landing plans, risk response capabilities, and whether the team matches the project requirements.  
* **Trust your engagement** : Are you a truly committed founder, passionate and committed to the project, and committed to growing your innovative business in the United Kingdom?

The interview with the sponsor agency for the Innovation Visa is a key step for you to demonstrate your professionalism, credibility, and dedication. Please remember the core idea: before the interview, the sponsor agency will look through your materials (business plan and financial model \+ personal information) to find **the elements of "being able to succeed"** ; and **the interview itself is to find evidence that can prove that you " cannot succeed"** .  
Therefore, you need to go beyond just submitting a business plan to respond with **vivid narration** and **strong evidence** , and make the reviewer trust that you are the **real leader and actual executor of the** project.  
By fully preparing and clearly communicating your business ideas and execution potential, you will be able to demonstrate your ability to innovate and successfully operate a business in the United Kingdom in all aspects, thus gaining assurance.

## **8 Common Mistakes in Guarantee Interviews**

Many entrepreneurs, even if their business plan is well written and their project has potential, may still be rejected in the interview process of guarantee agencies. This is not a problem with the project itself, but because of **unclear expression, inadequate preparation, or leaving an unprofessional impression on the reviewer** . Here are the 8 most common mistakes in guarantee agency interviews and how to understand them:

#### **Mistake 1: Only able to memorize drafts, not understanding business logic**

* Reviewers will ask about the details of the project, such as **pricing methods, user sources, data basis,** etc.  
* If you can't explain these details clearly, the reviewer will think you **don't have founder thinking** , but more like "someone packaged to apply for a visa".  
* The core criterion for innovation visa is **the founder's ability** . If you cannot prove that you are the **leader and actual executor** of the plan, you will be directly rejected.

#### **Mistake 2: Innovative answers are vague**

* When asked how to prove that your solution is more advanced than the existing solution in the United Kingdom, if you only use vague terms such as "AI, blockchain, platformization" without specifically explaining how to solve real problems, or without clearly explaining "why others can't do it" or "why users will switch to your solution", this is a problem.  
* The requirement for "innovation" in the United Kingdom Innovation Visa is to be able to **solve real problems more effectively and commercially viable with new methods** You don't need to be "unique in the world", but you must \*\* be "better than existing \+ able to clearly express this" \*\*.  
* Vague expressions will make it difficult for the guarantee agency to determine whether you truly understand the project or are just "riding on popular vocabulary". If the innovative points cannot clearly convince the reviewer, the project may be regarded as a "skin-changing plan" that does not meet the risk preference of the guarantee agency.

#### **Mistake 3: Unclear interpretation of key data**

* The reviewer will ask how your revenue forecast is calculated, market data sources, etc.  
* If your answer is "calculated by business consultants or accountants" or simply states "the industry has great potential", it indicates that you are not clear about the **revenue model or its hypothetical logic** .  
* The guarantor will consider that the applicant did not **lead the development of the business model** .

#### **Mistake 4: Not extending the question, the answer stays on the surface**

* When asked how to deal with potential problems such as poor customer feedback or lower conversion rates than expected, if you only answer "I will continue to optimize products or services and adjust according to market conditions", this will be considered as a **vague answer and lack of specific measures** .  
* This shows your **lack of risk response and product iteration capabilities** .

#### **Mistake 5: Ambiguous motivation looks like "immigration-oriented".**

* The reviewer will ask, 'Why did you choose to start a business in the United Kingdom? Why do you have to do this project in the United Kingdom?'  
* If you answer "The environment in the United Kingdom is stable, I like the United Kingdom", this will be considered a "lifestyle applicant" by the guarantee agency.  
* The Innovation Visa is a work visa, and the sponsoring agency will **reject the signal of "starting a business for immigration"** .

#### **Mistake 6: Completely copying the language of the proposal, lacking natural expression**

* If you read a business plan or roadshow throughout the interview, the content will appear **formatted, stiff, and emotionless** .  
* This is perceived as a **lack of internalized thinking and a real sense of ownership** . The interview assesses whether you really understand the logic, not whether you can memorize it.

#### **Mistake 7: Ignoring the "gray areas" not explained clearly in the proposal.**

* The reviewer will ask questions about unclear aspects of the business plan, such as early user acquisition methods and initial contact with cooperative relationships.  
* If you are unable to provide clear answers or additional information, vague answers will **amplify the reviewer's doubts** .  
* The interview is a great opportunity to supplement the incomplete parts of the proposal and demonstrate your ability as an entrepreneur to **think clearly and have begun preliminary preparation work** .

#### **Mistake 8: Showing excessive reliance on external resources and a lack of self-judgment**

* The reviewer will ask you what information you mainly referred to when deciding on the project, and which key decisions you personally made.  
* If you rely too much on the advice of a business advisor or market reports, and cannot clearly indicate the important judgments or reasons you make, you will be identified as **more like an executor than a leader** .  
* Business model, pricing method, cooperation strategy and other **key decisions should be led by the applicant** .

## **49 Common Questions for Guarantee Interviews**

The interview of the guarantee agency is a key link in applying for an innovation visa. Its **essential logic is to verify the authenticity of the applicant as a founder and the actual execution ability of their business plan** The reviewers aim to comprehensively understand your project, ability, market insight and landing plan in the United Kingdom through the following types of questions, in order to judge whether you meet the three core verification goals of "true founder", "profound grasp of business details" and "credible and feasible execution of landing logic".

1. **Project Core and Innovation**

This type of question aims to understand the basic situation of your project and its unique value in the market, especially its "innovation".

#### **1.1 Project Overview**

* **Please introduce your project** . The reviewer expects you to clearly and concisely articulate the core of the project and use real-life examples to illustrate your project model.  
* **What problem does your product/service solve? Why does this problem matter?** The focus is on finding accurate industry pain points, analyzing their differentiated value, and proving that entrepreneurial opportunities are real.  
* **Who is the target customer? How do you define the ideal user portrait?** It is necessary to clarify who your perfect customer is, avoid answering "everyone", and refine the customer's age, purchasing power, region, gender and other dimensions.  
* **What stage is your product currently in? Any prototypes, MVPs, or early adopters?** Evaluate project progress, including technical feasibility, such as whether a prototype has been built and is working properly.

#### **1.2 Innovation and unique advantages**

* **Please specify where your project "innovates"?** This requires you to clarify how the project is more advanced than existing solutions in the United Kingdom. Innovation does not need to be "globally unique", but must be "better than existing" and can clearly express this.  
* **What are the differences or advantages of your solution compared to products in the existing market?** You need to clearly position yourself, objectively analyze your competitors, and reflect your core advantages and differentiated play.  
* **Have you used new technologies, new models, or unique processes?** Emphasize how new methods can more effectively solve real problems and be commercially viable.  
* **Do you have intellectual property, patents, know-how, or advantages that are hard to replicate?** Learn about your long-term competitive edge and competitive barriers.

#### **1.3 Product and technical details**

* **How do you know your product is viable?** (Technically viable, e.g. whether there is a prototype, whether it works?)  
* **How do you know if your product is feasible within budget?**  
* **Your business plan mentions... Please provide proof of the products you have developed, as well as proof of how the software and hardware work.**  
* **Who will develop \[product name\]?**  
* **Please provide more technical details.** (1-2 pages description of technical details)  
* **What devices do end users need to have to use your product?**

2. **Market insights and business models**

This type of question tests your understanding of the industry and business model, as well as its potential in the United Kingdom market.

#### **2.1 Target Market and Users**

* **How big is your target market and ceiling?** (How to derive the method of market ceiling size) This requires you to clearly calculate the revenue model and hypothesis logic, not just say "the industry has great potential".  
* **What is the development trend and concentration of your track?** (Concentration determines competition and landscape) The reviewer wants to know if you have a macro understanding of the industry and how your project can gain opportunities in this landscape.  
* **How do customers discover your product? How do you promote it?** Ask about user sources, acquisition channels, and costs.  
* **What are the core indicators of your business?** (Evaluation indicators that conform to industry consensus)

#### **2.2 Profit model and growth strategy**

* **What is your revenue model? How will customers pay for your product/service?** Clarify whether your business closed loop is established.  
* **What is your profit model exactly?**  
* **What are the growth factors in your business model?** (Growth drivers)  
* **What is the business progress reflected behind the operational data of your business?** (Don't just talk about numbers)

#### **2.3 Competitive analysis and barriers**

* **What are your competitors?** (how to position clearly)  
* **How far have your competitors developed? Why do you still have a chance?** (Understanding of competing products)  
* **What are the advantages of your project compared to the original product/service?** (How much better than the original solution) To avoid belittling competitors, you should objectively understand and explain the differentiated play.  
* **What is the long-term competitive edge of your business?** (competitive barriers anticipated).

3. **Team capability and execution plan**

These questions focus on your abilities as a founder, team composition, and specific planning for project implementation.

#### **3.1 Founder and team background**

* How did you come up with the idea of doing this project? What was your original intention for starting a business? (What is the core driving force behind your entrepreneurship?)  
* How is your team? Do you have the ability to do this project well? (How well does your team's ability match?)  
* Do you have any experience in starting a business or running a company?  
* How does your experience relate to product development?  
* What directly useful skills and experiences will you bring?  
* Where will the other necessary skills and experience come from?

#### **3.2 Business Development and Milestones**

* What is the goal for the first year of your project? How to achieve it specifically? Specific measures should be provided instead of vague answers.  
* What are the expected business plans and milestones in the next 3 years?  
* When do you expect to achieve profitability?  
* How long has your project been in operation? How profitable is it? (Determine if the single-point model is running smoothly)  
* What are the current per customer transactions, customer numbers, sales, and profits of your project? (Determine the current status of the project)  
* How do you plan to expand your business in the future? Is it limited to the United Kingdom? Can it be internationalized?

#### **3.3 Recruitment and job creation**

* What positions will you recruit for? How many jobs do you expect to create?  
* Please provide the recruitment plan of your planned United Kingdom company.  
* What skills/experience and qualifications would you recruit?

4. **United Kingdom market and compliance**

These questions focus on your reasons for choosing the United Kingdom, your understanding of the United Kingdom environment, and your preparation for long-term development in the United Kingdom.

#### **4.1 Reasons for choosing the United Kingdom**

* **Why choose to start a business in the United Kingdom instead of other countries?** Your answer should focus on the business opportunities and the fit of the project with the United Kingdom market, avoiding giving "immigration-oriented" answers such as "the United Kingdom environment is stable, I like the United Kingdom".  
* **Where do you see the business opportunities for this project in the United Kingdom?** This requires you to have a deep understanding of the United Kingdom market and be able to articulate its uniqueness.  
* **Why is there an opportunity to start a business now?** (What are the reasons for the right time now)

#### **4.2 Understanding and integration into the United Kingdom market**

* **Do you understand the United Kingdom market, regulations, customer behavior, etc.?** The judges will examine your familiarity with the local business environment in the United Kingdom.  
* **Do you currently have a network of local partners or resources in the United Kingdom?**  
* **Where do you plan to register the company? Why?**  
* **Do you have a plan to adapt to life in the United Kingdom (tax, banking, etc.)?**

#### **4.3 Risk Response and Alternative Plans**

* **If your plan is rejected/failed, what is your Plan B?** It examines your risk response ability and contingency plan.

5. **Supplementary material requirements**

In addition to oral Q & A, guarantee agencies usually require you to provide or confirm some key written materials.

* **Letters of recommendation.**  
* **Your resume.**  
* **Your education and work experience prove it.**  
* **Provide your analysis of competitors and partners.**

![][image10]

# **Main Course 2: Pitch Deck Structure Model and Lean Canvas**

## **10 Minute Pitch Frame**

An excellent Pitch Deck is the key to clearly and efficiently presenting your business ideas to guarantee agencies or investors. The following is a breakdown and key points of a standard 10-minute Pitch framework.  
![][image11]

1. **Opening positioning (summary of project highlights in one sentence)**

At the beginning of the pitch, use the most concise sentence to **grab the audience's attention** and quickly convey your core values. This should not be your marketing slogan, but a 5-7 word corporate explanation that allows strangers who do not know your business to quickly understand what you do. This "one-sentence introduction" should extract the brightest point of the project and arouse the interest of the other party.

* **Core points** :  
  * Refined: Usually limited to **12 words or less** , such as the "Header" section.  
  * Clear: Let strangers quickly understand your business.  
  * Engaging: Stimulate the other party's interest in continuing to learn.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * The founder of Uber once described their service as "you just press **a button and a car will come to pick you up** ". This intuitively demonstrates the convenience of the service.  
  * If your company's business is to help founders with financing, an opening positioning can be "We help founders **navigate the financing process** ."  
  * The founders of the early school network could simply say, "I'm doing the **Chinese version of Facebook** ," which quickly made investors understand its model.  
2. **Pain point description (specific problem \+ opportunity)**

This section aims to show that your project solves a **real, sufficiently "painful" problem in the** market.

* **Core points** :  
  * Specific problem: Describe a pain point that your market or customers are experiencing, which should be a " **painful inconvenience** " such as a waste of money or time.  
  * Based on facts: These questions should be based on real data and sources, not just your personal opinions.  
  * Discovering Opportunities: Sometimes, you may not be solving a "problem", but rather seizing a "business opportunity", such as the rise of Emerging Markets.  
  * Refined expression: Industry issues are usually presented in the form **of 3 key points** , each point no more than **8 words** .  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * Uber's early Pitch Deck described the problems in the taxi market in 2008: **"Mainly using old, inefficient technology"** , **"Relying on radio, unable to communicate in both directions"** , **"Taking a taxi by'hand 'or phone"** .  
  * In addition, it also points out problems with the taxi operating license system, such as \*\* "taxi monopoly leads to a decrease in service quality" **, and** "expensive license fees and low driver income" \*\*.  
  * For the "Urban Gardening App" project, its pain points may be: **"Urban space is limited and difficult to expand"** , **"Gardening knowledge is scarce and difficult to get started"** , **"Plant diseases and pests are difficult to identify"** .  
3. **Solution summary (your core innovation)**

This section is a **direct response** to your questions and highlights your **innovation** .

* **Core points** :  
  * Core scenario: Outline how your platform or service **solves the problem abstractly** .  
  * Product Display: Maximize the space to showcase your product's appearance, working principle, or breakthrough technology.  
  * Innovation: Clearly articulate your innovation points and explain how your new method **more effectively solves real problems** , as well as "why others can't do it" **or** "why users will switch to your approach". Avoid using vague terms such as "AI, blockchain", and instead specifically reflect the problem-solving process.  
  * Value proposition: Clarify your unique value proposition (usually **within 12 words** ) and the specific benefits that the product can bring (usually **3 key points** , each point **within 8 words** ).  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * Uber's solution is \*\* "One-Click Car Service" **, achieving** "Fast \+ Efficient On-Demand Car Service" **. Its core differentiation lies in** "Member-only service" **,** "One-Click Taxi \- 'Pick me up here in 5 minutes'" **,** "High-tech Solution \- Location-based Automatic Dispatch" \*\*.  
  * The solutions of "Urban Gardening App" include: **"Space Optimization Tool"** , **"Plant Care Reminder"** , **"Pest Identification and Treatment"** .  
  * Its unique value proposition may be: **"Efficiently grow a green life in a small space"** . Product benefits can be: **"Reasonable layout of space utilization"** , **"Intelligent reminder of plant care"** , **"Quick identification of pests and diseases"** .  
  * You can attach a **demo photo** or video of the product for visual display.  
4. **Competitive analysis (your unique strengths)**

This section is designed to demonstrate to investors your deep understanding of the market environment and competition landscape, and to highlight your unique strengths and competitive strategies.

* **Key points:**  
  * **Understanding the nature of competition:** not only to identify **direct competitors** (offering the same or similar products/services, targeting the same customer group, such as Anthropic v Open AI), but also to consider **indirect competitors** (offering different products/services but solving the same customer needs or problems, such as Chat GPT v Google Search). Even if the company does not have your technology, it may still constitute a competitor.  
  * **Demonstrate market insights:** Your competitive analysis should focus on your unique understanding of the market and your deeper insights than your competitors. This helps show investors that you understand the risks, understand your value proposition and customer needs, and can tell a compelling "why now" story.  
  * **Highlight unique advantages:** Clearly articulate your **unique value proposition (USP) and hard-to-replicate "Secret Sauce" or "Unfair Advantage"** , which are unique to your company and not previously mentioned in the slides. This may include **proprietary Image Recognition Technology** , **partnerships with local nurseries** , patents, or unique processes.  
  * **Objective analysis and differentiation:** Founders should **objectively acknowledge the advantages of competitors** , and clearly explain your **differentiated play** , so that investors believe that you have the ability to defeat competitors. Avoid belittling competitors or overconfidence.  
  * **Demonstrate competitive barriers:** Explain what your business's **long-term competitive edge** is and how competitive barriers determine industry concentration to effectively resist competition from newcomers.  
* **Cases and Examples:**  
  * In the competitive analysis slide, you can use the form of a **matrix or quadrant chart** to visually show your positioning with your competitors.  
  * In Uber's early BP, through pictures and short text, it compared the traditional taxi industry's **pain points (old technology, low efficiency, driver picking, license monopoly, etc.)** , and explained Uber's **concept (fast \+ efficient, on-demand service, high-tech automatic dispatch) and core differentiation elements** .  
  * When answering investor questions, specify how your solution \*\* is "more advanced than existing solutions in the United Kingdom" **, or** "better than existing solutions" \*\*.  
* **Investor focus:**  
  * Investors will ask who your competitors are, how developed they are, and why you still have opportunities.  
  * They will want to know how you have proven that the product is technically feasible and how your experience relates to product development.  
  * Do you own intellectual property, patents, or proprietary technology?  
5. **Market validation (real demand \+ data support)**

This section aims to prove to the audience that your product has a **large enough market and real customer needs** .

* **Core points** :  
  * Target customers: Identify who your ideal customers are and create a precise profile of them (such as age, purchasing power, geographic location, gender), instead of talking about "everyone" in general.  
  * Market size: Quantify the market potential through **total addressable market (TAM), serviceable addressable market (SAM), and accessible market (SOM)** . You need to show how to calculate these data and explain the source of the data. TAM is the total upper limit, SAM is the actual serviceable range, and SOM is the share that the company can obtain in the short term.  
  * Market growth: If your company is in the financing stage, you need to show **user growth and operational data (Traction)** . Charts often tell a better story than individual numbers.  
  * Verification basis: Provide case studies or user feedback to prove that your solution has been adopted by real customers and generates value.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * Line's IPO roadshow showcased its leading position in four key markets **: Japan, Taiwan, Thailand, and Indonesia** (MAU data). It also graphed Japan's smartphone penetration rate and the market's growth potential in digital/mobile advertising.  
  * Uber's early Pitch Deck showcased the **$4.20 billion** US taxi/limousine market and noted that the **top four companies accounted for only 22% of revenue** , suggesting low market concentration and huge opportunities.  
  * "Urban Gardening App" can clearly define its customer group as: **"novice urban gardener"** , **"senior urban gardener"** , **"urban nursery and gardening store"** .  
  * When calculating TAM, SAM, and SOM, it is recommended to use both **top-down (Top-down) and bottom-up (Bottom-up)** methods for estimation and comparison, and record all data sources.  
6. **Business model (how to make money)**

Clearly explain your **profit model** .

* **Core points** :  
  * Revenue sources: Clearly explain your revenue model, such as subscription fees, usage-based payments, commission-based payments, or other methods.  
  * Cost structure: Outline the main cost components.  
  * Business closed loop: Ensure that your profit model can form a complete business closed loop.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * TMT Seeds business model includes multiple revenue sources: **C2C transaction matching service fee (10% commission)** , App/official account **advertising revenue** , **SaaS product revenue** , **platform operation and maintenance revenue** , **merchant entry platform service fee** , and even **2B data services** .  
  * The revenue stream for "Urban Gardening App" can be: **"In-App Purchases (Premium Features) "** , **"Affiliate Marketing (Commission on Product Sales) "** , **"Subscription Model (Member Services) "** , **"Advertising Revenue"** .  
  * Line's business model evolution shows a diversified monetization path from **stickers (Stickers) to content (Content) and then to instant message ads (Messenger Ads)** , and demonstrates the mature monetization capabilities of its content platform and advertising revenue growth.  
7. **Execution ability (team \+ resource advantage)**

Show that you and your team are **the best people to drive the success of this project** .

* **Core points** :  
  * Team Composition: Describe how the **core competencies and experience** of team members match the project requirements. You are financing to execute existing skills, not to recruit core skills.  
  * Competitive advantage: Identify your team's **core strengths and "unfair advantages" over** competitors.  
  * Past experience: Share your or your team members' relevant experience in starting or running a company.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * Luo Jun, founder of Tujia.com, told his experience (studying accounting in college, becoming a top salesperson after graduation, exposure to a large number of real estate resources, love for the hotel industry, and finding a suitable Internet product manager) to prove that he **has the ability to make projects and resource integration advantages** .  
  * The "unfair advantage" of the "Urban Gardening App" lies in: **"Proprietary Image Recognition Technology"** (accurate identification of plant diseases) and "partnership with local nurseries" (offering exclusive discounts and expert advice).  
  * During the interview, the reviewer will ask how your experience is relevant to product development, as well as what other skills are required and where they come from.  
8. **Expansion path (short, medium and long-term goals)**

Elaborate on the **future development plan and potential of** your project.

* **Core points** :  
  * Milestones: Set specific business plans and milestones for the **short term (Year 1\)** , medium term (3 years) **and** long term (Internationalization).  
  * Growth strategy: Explain how you will **acquire early customers** and drive business growth.  
  * Recruitment plan: If you plan to expand in the United Kingdom, you need to specify which positions will be recruited and the expected number of jobs to be created.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * Uber's early plan is **to start from San Francisco** , soon cover Manhattan, and **plans to expand to Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston and other cities** , covering 50% of the US market.  
  * Line's IPO roadshow showcased its "enticing growth opportunities": **expanding its user base and enhancing engagement** (mainly in Japan, Taiwan, Thailand, Indonesia), **developing content and life platforms** , eventually **evolving into smart portals** , and looking ahead to **future markets in South East Asia, the Middle East, and the rest of the world** .  
  * In the financing requirement, you need to clearly explain the **financing amount, fund use** , and how these funds can help you **reach the next financing milestone** and avoid getting stuck in the "middle stage".  
9. **Closing emphasis (Founder Commitment \+ UK Fit)**

At the end, reinforce your **level of investment in** the project and its **fit with the United Kingdom market** .

* **Core points** :  
  * Founder Engagement: Emphasize that you will be **fully committed to** this project. The judges will verify your entrepreneurial motivation and ensure that you are here for business opportunities rather than simply immigration.  
  * United Kingdom Market Fit: Explain why you chose to start a business in the United Kingdom, as well as your understanding of the United Kingdom market, regulation, and customer behavior. Avoid giving the signal of "starting a business for immigration", as the Innovation Visa is a type of work visa, and guarantee agencies will reject applicants with this signal.  
  * Financing needs: **Clearly state your financing needs** , including the amount of financing, financing rounds, use of funds, and how these funds can help you reach the next financing milestone. Although this part is transactional, it is usually included at the end of the roadshow.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * The interviewer will directly ask you "Why did you choose to start a business in the United Kingdom instead of other countries?" Your answer should focus on the business opportunities and the fit of the project with the United Kingdom market.  
  * You need to demonstrate an understanding of the United Kingdom market, regulation, and customer behavior, and even whether there is a local partner or resource network in the United Kingdom.

The above is the detailed structural model of Pitch Deck, combined with the guidance and examples from the source, hoping to help you better prepare.  
---

Now delve into the "How" questions behind your business idea, which requires you to demonstrate deep logical thinking and strategic planning skills. The Lean Business Canvas and Industry Anticipation Canvas are key tools to help you think systematically and articulate these "How" s.

## **Lean Business Canvas**

The Lean Business Canvas is a simple yet powerful tool made up of nine core modules designed to help you tease out your business model and ensure your business logic is clear, complete, and viable. In Pitch, being able to fluidly articulate every part of the canvas means you have a deep understanding and ownership of your business idea.  
Lean Business Canvas is a nine-building tool designed to help entrepreneurs **efficiently tease out** and **analyze** their business models to create products that customers really need and avoid wasting valuable resources. It advocates the use of lightweight, dynamic models for extremely uncertain environments.

### **The nine building blocks of Lean Canvas include:**

* **Problem** : Identify the **core pain points and challenges** customers are currently facing.  
* **Solution** : Describe how your product or service **specifically solves** the above problem and the core functionality or tools it provides.  
* **Unique Value Proposition (UVP)** : A concise statement that **summarizes the unique benefits your product or service brings to customers** and sets it apart.  
* **Unfair Advantage** : Refers to an **advantage that is difficult for competitors to replicate or surpass** , which may be your proprietary technology, unique partnerships, or other core competencies.  
* **Customer segmentation (Customer Segments)** : Identify the **specific customer groups** your product or service targets, including their characteristics and needs.  
* **Key Metrics** : Identify key data and quantifiable metrics to **measure business progress and success** .  
* **Channels** : Describes how you will **distribute and promote** your product or service to reach your target customers.  
* **Cost Structure** : Lists all the **major expenses** required to run the business, including development, marketing, servers, partnerships, and customer support.  
* **Revenue Streams** : Explain how your business will **generate revenue** , such as in-app purchases, subscriptions, or advertising.

### **How to use Lean Canvas :**

Entrepreneurs should **frequently create and adjust** Lean Canvas. This involves a "Build-Measure-Learn" loop. By testing multiple iterations and publicly soliciting customer feedback, you can help you **create products that customers really need** , and **avoid wasting valuable resources** . Although analyzing data can confirm the existence of problems, **real human customers** can provide solutions.  
![][image12]

## **The anticipated Industry Prediction Canvas**

The Industry Anticipate Canvas provides a scientific thinking framework to help entrepreneurs identify and evaluate industry opportunities. It emphasizes the "A to B model", which is the evolution process from the current industry status (A) to the future stable state (B), as well as the factors driving these changes and the entrepreneurial opportunities they bring. This can help you answer the question "Why is there an opportunity to start a business now?"

1. **Quickly break down an industry (anticipated point 1: understand the current state of the industry point A)**

This is the basic work of industry analysis, which requires you to be able to break down the industry into a series of links, understand the upstream and downstream relationships, profit distribution, and the role and value of intermediaries.

* **Core points** :  
  * **Industrial chain disassembly** : understand what links there are within the industry, what upstream and downstream a company has, and what the relationship between them is.  
  * **Profit distribution** : Analyze the income composition and profit distribution of each link in the final retail price of the product.  
  * **Intermediary value** : Understand why intermediaries (such as wholesalers) make money and what risks and obligations (such as logistics, services, or funds) they assume.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * **The K12 education industry** can be broken down into teaching materials, teachers, sales, and student needs. Differences in the production of teaching materials, the emergence of online foreign teachers, new sales methods brought by WeChat Mini Program, and changes in online course content and cost structure may all bring new business models.  
  * **The fresh retail industry** 's A state is dominated by vegetable markets and supermarkets. The advantages of vegetable markets are cheap rent, low operating costs, and abundant SKUs, which can meet most needs.  
  * By visiting industry professionals and reading industry research reports, one can enhance their understanding of the industry chain.  
2. **Insight into the underlying reasons for industry change (anticipated point 2: capturing change)**

Identify the sudden changes that occur in key links in the industry, which are the root of entrepreneurial opportunities. Look for those "big changes" that can greatly affect life.

* **Core points** :  
  * **Types of changes** : demand-side changes, supply-side changes, new technology changes, policy changes, etc.  
  * **Systematic change** : It is not the huge change in a single link that can bring great opportunities, but the systemic change in the entire business model chain that can really change the industry.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * **Changes in the fresh retail industry** include:  
    * **User request changes** : rising consumption power, population concentration leading to high residential density (such as 4-50,000 households within two kilometers of China), and users' high requirements for convenience (accustomed to takeout delivered to their homes).  
    * **Production/supply chain changes** : China's supply chain is developing rapidly, the standardization of fresh food quality is improving, and the efficiency of cold chain and transportation is improving.  
    * **Mobile Internet impact** : WeChat covers elderly users, users can buy fresh food online; logistics distribution (end distribution) is mature, achieving next-day delivery or even half an hour delivery.  
    * **Policy changes** : The lack of supporting facilities for vegetable markets in new urban areas has led to supply-side changes.  
  * **SVN** : The developed countries or markets have run through the model, as the conditions mature, replicated to other markets or Non-Major Market, such as Wang Xing replicated the Silicon Valley model to China, and the Chinese model to South East Asia, Africa.  
3. **Anticipate the appearance of steady state B (anticipate point 3: think about the vision)**

After analyzing the current situation and changes in the industry, predict what kind of new stable state the industry will tend to in the future. This requires in-depth analysis combining user requests and business models.

* **Core points** :  
  * **Customer demand orientation** : Industry development is essentially to better meet customer needs under external restrictions.  
  * **Demand differentiation** : Understand that different client bases have different focuses on the demands of "more, faster, better, and cheaper" (quantity, speed, quality, price).  
  * **Limitations of the model** : Analyze what needs existing mainstream business models (such as vegetable markets, Community Group Buying, front warehouses) can meet and their limitations, and judge whether there is an optimal solution for "all-in-one".  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * **Fresh retail industry** 's future state B: Due to the contradictions and divergences in user requests (many, fast, good, and provincial), there is currently no industry that can lead comprehensively.  
    * **Traditional vegetable markets** satisfy the demand for "more", but the shopping experience and price transparency are poor.  
    * **Community Group Buying** meets the needs of "saving" (low price, low performance cost, less damage), but sacrifices "fast" and "many" (poor timeliness, limited SKU).  
    * **The front warehouse model** meets the needs of "fast" (fast fulfillment speed, convenience), but may sacrifice "many" (limited SKU due to limited area) or limited scalability.  
  * This means that the future of fresh retail may be a variety of models coexist, each serving different segmented client base and needs.  
4. **Analyze the industry change cycle (anticipate point 4: seize the opportunity)**

Determine the life cycle of the industry your project is in and choose the best entrepreneurial window to enter. Being too early may become a "martyr", while being too late may face fierce competition.

* **Core points** :  
  * **Ideal entrepreneurial window period** : enter before the industry outbreak, and accumulate core capabilities, resources and organizational capabilities at this stage, so as to seize opportunities when they come and establish themselves in subsequent competition.  
  * **Fault tolerance of large companies** : Unlike startups, large companies have higher fault tolerance in startup timing and can enter earlier or later.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * Around 2006, the first batch of domestic mobile internet start-up companies became "martyrs" due to the early stage of 3G. However, when the real outbreak period arrived from 2010 to 2012, most of these companies had already lost their opportunities.  
  * This is linked to the financing plan to ensure that the funds you raise are sufficient to support the company to reach the next financing milestone and avoid getting stuck in the "middle stage".  
5. **Analyze the magnitude of change (anticipated point 5: calculate the space)**

Quantify market potential and evaluate industry ceiling size. This is usually measured through total addressable market (TAM), serviceable addressable market (SAM), and accessible market (SOM), which is the focus of investors' attention, especially for USD funds.

* **Core points** :  
  * **The best time to start a business** : enter a future huge, currently low-scale but fast-growing industry.  
  * **Market size indicators** :  
    * **Total addressable market (TAM)** : The maximum market potential of the product/service worldwide, the total revenue that can be sold by all suppliers.  
    * **Serviceable addressable market (SAM)** : Total sales in the area you can actually serve.  
    * **Accessible Market (SOM)** : The amount of sales your company can achieve in the short term is a realistic target.  
  * **Data Acquisition and Estimation** : Estimate through open source data (such as industry analysis reports, consulting firm reports, industry media, etc.) and record all sources. It is recommended to use both "top-down" and "bottom-up" methods for estimation and comparison, and continuously iterate and improve.  
  * **Importance** : Market size is the key for investors to judge whether the project is "risk scale" and whether it can obtain sufficient returns.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * Uber's early Pitch Deck showed the US taxi/limousine market at $4.20 billion and pointed out that the top four companies accounted for only 22% of revenue, suggesting a huge market opportunity.  
  * The Line IPO roadshow showcased MAU data for the four major markets of Japan, Taiwan, Thailand, and Indonesia, as well as the growth potential of the Japanese smartphone penetration rate and digital/mobile advertising market.  
  * In the pitch, it is necessary to clearly explain how you calculate the market ceiling and have rigorous deduction and calculation methods.  
6. **Analysis of future concentration (anticipated point 6: enhancing competitiveness)**

Estimate the future market concentration trend of the industry and how your company can enhance competitiveness and gain market share in this change. Industries with high barriers to entry are more likely to form high concentration.

* **Core points** :  
  * **Concentration Definition** : Measure whether players in the industry are concentrated or dispersed.  
  * **Best Trend** : The ideal situation is that the market is fragmented now, but there is a chance to form a dominant situation in the future (i.e. from low concentration to high concentration). Although the competition is fierce, there is a chance to grow in the future and be more favored by investors.  
  * **Barriers determine concentration** : the higher the industry barriers, the easier it is to resist competition from newcomers, obtain a large market share, and even form a monopoly.  
  * **Understanding Competition** : Demonstrate what you know about your competitors and why you still have a chance to win in the market.  
* **Cases and Examples** :  
  * Instant messaging, e-commerce platforms and other fields have formed a highly concentrated "721" pattern (the top three companies occupy 70%, 20%, and 10% of the market share). If you enter these highly concentrated fields now, the feasibility is basically zero.  
  * Although the catering industry has a huge market, it is extremely fragmented. No company can occupy more than 10% of the market share, making it a low-concentration industry.  
  * In Pitch, objectively analyze the competitive environment, highlight your core strengths and differentiated strategies, and make investors believe that you have the ability to defeat your competitors. Avoid belittling competitors, as investors are smart and this may backfire.

Through the systematic thinking of Lean Business Canvas and Industry Anticipation Canvas, you can not only clearly articulate the "What" of your business, but more importantly, you can deeply answer the "How" and "Why you do it". This structured way of thinking will help you demonstrate your professionalism, insight, and execution ability as a founder in pitches and interviews.
